description: Three types of dangerous toys flagged by Trouble in Toyland, and the legal options Georgia parents have if their child has been injured by a toy.
shortAnswer: Normally, a products liability claim is going to be the best option for parents. In Georgia, product liability is centered upon O.C.G.A. Section 51-1-11. To have a strong case, you must be able to prove fault on the part of the toy manufacturer.

faq.q: What types of dangerous toys does the Trouble in Toyland report warn parents about?
faq.a: The most recent edition of Trouble in Toyland identifies three types of toys parents should be aware of: toys with easily identifiable hazards, toys with hidden hazards, and toys that have been recalled but are still for sale.

faq.q: How can I tell if a toy is a choking hazard for my child?
faq.a: Trouble in Toyland recommends using a toilet paper roll to gauge whether an object poses a choking hazard. If the object fits easily through the center of the roll, it is too small. Of all toys, balloons are the leading cause of death by suffocation.

faq.q: Do I have a case if my young child swallowed a toy marketed only for teens and adults?
faq.a: If your child gets their hands on and swallows small marbles that are marketed strictly for teens and adults, I am afraid that you have no case. However, if the manufacturer's advertising neglected to make clear what age groups the marbles were appropriate for, they are partially responsible for injuries resulting from small children playing with the product.

faq.q: What legal theories can a Georgia parent use besides O.C.G.A. Section 51-1-11?
faq.a: While O.C.G.A. Section 51-1-11 is the basis for most products liability claims, there are other legal options open to a parent whose child is injured by a dangerous toy. A plaintiff can rely on negligence, strict liability, and warranty theories.
